content: Some individuals may have limited understanding of health and treatment-related information, while others may express concerns about potential side effects of treatments. When these challenges are compounded by social and structural barriers, they can significantly impede decision-making processes related to seeking healthcare, initiating treatment, and reducing disease risks. Healthcare services should consistently provide accurate, clear, evidence-based, and non-judgmental information to people who inject drugs (PWID) regarding the prevention, care, and treatment of tuberculosis (TB), HIV, and viral hepatitis. This information can also be disseminated through community networks and peer workers. It is essential that such information addresses PWID’s concerns about comorbidities, treatment side effects, and social and structural barriers, including fears of stigma, discrimination, and criminalization. Healthcare providers, as well as prison guards and management in correctional settings, may lack adequate knowledge of the health and social care needs of PWID. To address this, healthcare services in both community and prison settings should provide training to staff to enhance their understanding of PWID’s needs. This will improve the capacity to prevent and treat HIV, TB, and viral hepatitis among this population. PWID often experience multiple comorbidities, frequently within contexts of marginalization and deprivation. The prevalence of TB, HIV, viral hepatitis, and other infectious diseases is high among PWID, as are mental health conditions. Integrating healthcare services can significantly improve access to collaborative TB/HIV activities for the general population and provide opportunities for person-centered prevention, care, and treatment for PWID, who have complex health and social care needs. Such integrated services also promote better communication, multidisciplinary care, and increased efficiency and cost-effectiveness. Where feasible, programs should aim to deliver integrated services for PWID in ways that are informed by their needs and foster trust in service delivery settings and providers. When integration is not possible, strong linkages among health and social services working with PWID should be established and maintained. The process of updating the WHO 2008 policy guidelines followed the procedures recommended by the WHO Guidelines Review Committee (GRC). All recommendations and guidance in the document are derived from existing WHO guidance and were developed according to GRC processes. A Joint Steering Group, comprising focal points from WHO, UNAIDS, and UNODC, was formed to oversee the process. An External Guideline Group, including policymakers, experts in TB, HIV, viral hepatitis, and drug-use services, donor agencies, and representatives from PWID networks, was also established. Declarations of interest were submitted by all members and reviewed to ensure no conflicts of interest. The Joint Steering Group prepared a draft framework and list of recommendations, which were circulated to the External Guideline Group for feedback. Revisions were incorporated, and the policy was then reviewed by internal and external peer reviewers. Comments were discussed, and the document was finalized by the process coordinators. The goal of integrating collaborative TB and HIV services within a comprehensive harm reduction package is to reduce morbidity and mortality from TB and HIV-associated TB among PWID, as well as to address other comorbidities associated with drug use. Objectives include establishing mechanisms for integrated service delivery, reducing the joint burden of TB, HIV, viral hepatitis, and other comorbidities, and ensuring access to comprehensive, people-centered care. Key recommendations include setting up a national multisectoral coordinating body with representation from key stakeholders, including PWID networks, to oversee governance, planning, implementation, and resource mobilization for integrated services. This body should operate at all levels and ensure collaboration across sectors. It should also address governance issues, such as resource allocation and responsibilities for financing and implementing joint plans. Critical enablers for equitable access to care for PWID include revising laws and policies to support the implementation of integrated, evidence-based healthcare services, decriminalizing drug use, and addressing stigma, discrimination, and violence against PWID. Health services should be made accessible and acceptable to PWID, based on principles of medical ethics and the right to health. Programs should also work towards community empowerment and meaningful involvement of PWID in service delivery and policy-making processes.
